title: a year of service designed
hook: a graduation speech in an Upanishad tells students to treat the guest as a god

segments.voice: Yesterday, a year of service designed, piece three: the gift sorted three ways, and the four questions: why, what back, when, to whom. Did you plan one gift and ask them? Day nine hundred seventy-two.
screen: `THE GIFT.` · `WHY, WHAT BACK, WHEN, TO WHOM.`

segments.voice: Students are about to leave their teacher's house. Their study is done. And before they go, the teacher gives them a last talk, the kind of advice you'd hope to hear at any graduation. Speak the truth. Follow dharma. Don't neglect your study. Don't neglect your duty to the gods and the ancestors. And then a run of short lines that some Hindus still know by heart. That farewell talk sits in the Taittiriya Upanishad, and one of its lines gives today's piece of a year of service: the people who come through your door.
screen: `THE STUDENTS ARE LEAVING.` → `THE TEACHER'S LAST TALK.` → `THE PEOPLE AT YOUR DOOR.`

segments.voice: The run of lines goes like this, in paraphrase. Let your mother be a god to you. Let your father be a god to you. Let your teacher be a god to you. Let your guest be a god to you. In Sanskrit that last one is atithi devo bhava. Atithi is the guest. Devo bhava, be as a god. Notice who's on that list. Mother, father, teacher: people you owe something to, people who came first. And then the guest, who may be a stranger, someone you owe nothing at all. The Upanishad puts them in the same row. The same farewell talk goes on to giving: give with faith, not without faith, give with modesty, give with understanding. So the teacher sets hospitality and giving side by side, as a life's practice rather than a one-time act. What does that look like in a year of service? It may be the piece of the plan closest to home. A spare chair at the table. The colleague nobody invites to lunch. The new family on the street. A cousin in town for a hospital stay who needs a place to sleep. The tradition doesn't ask for a grand gesture. It asks for a door that opens, and for the person who walks through it to be received with the care you'd give to something holy. That's a high bar. It's also service that can happen without leaving home.
screen: `MOTHER, FATHER, TEACHER, GUEST.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST AS A GOD.` · `HOSPITALITY AND GIVING, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `A DOOR THAT OPENS.` · then, large: `RECEIVE THEM AS HOLY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind your own front door, or the door of the room where you spend your days. See it open. Now let one person come through it: someone who's actually likely to come by in the next few months, a neighbor, a coworker, a relative, a friend of your child. Watch how you'd usually greet them. Then, without changing anything outward, let the greeting deepen inside, as if receiving someone who matters more than you knew. Breathe there. If you pray, you can see the one you pray to in that guest. The bell holds the time.
A year of service designed. Today's piece is the guest: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you.
screen: `A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a year of service designed. Today, choose one person to invite in this year, for a meal, a coffee, a night, and put a date near it on the calendar. Day nine hundred seventy-two.

screen: `DAY 972 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED.`

howItsDone: Hospitality has a respected place in Hindu homes, and the Taittiriya Upanishad's line atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you, is a saying some families teach their children.

fork.setup: you're the teacher. your students are leaving to start their lives. after truth and dharma, who do you tell them to treat as a god?
options: mother, father, teacher, and the guest.
no one; gods are for temples.
fork.reveal: the Taittiriya Upanishad's farewell talk ends that list with the guest: atithi devo bhava.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you, from the Taittiriya Upanishad.

trapdoor: what you thought: hospitality is good manners.
what it means: the Upanishad puts the guest beside mother, father and teacher: let them be a god to you.
what a scholar hears: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11, the teacher's farewell to departing students, which goes on to how to give: with faith, modesty and understanding.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.1–1.11.3 (the farewell talk: speak the truth, follow dharma; mother, father, teacher, guest as gods; give with faith, modesty and understanding)

notes: Editor: cut the atithi 'without a set date' gloss (an etymology the cited text does not give) and the unsupported 'one of the few kinds of service' claim.
Paraphrase of Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (Shiksha Valli, anuvaka 11). Confirm the order of the lines and the giving instructions (shraddhaya deyam, ashraddhaya adeyam, hriya deyam, samvida deyam).

'In a traditional reading, a guest is a person who arrives without a set date' reflects the common gloss of atithi as one without a fixed tithi; presented as a reading, not an etymology. Keeper: keep or cut.
'Some Hindus still know by heart' and 'some families teach their children' are soft general claims; confirm acceptable.
Original-language line is written atithidevo bhava as in the text's sandhi; confirm spelling.
